newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Rebel-held Colombian troops flown in for release.
newsitem.headline: Rebel-held Colombian troops flown in for release.

text.p: Scores of soldiers taken prisoner last August arrived in this jungle town on Sunday for their release at a ceremony orchestrated by Marxist-led rebels.

The handover of the 60 soldiers captured in the southwestern province of Putumayo marks the end of Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis, a drama largely overshadowed by the siege of the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.
Ten marines captured in a firefight in January in the northwestern province of Choco were also to be freed at the ceremony.

The soldiers began arriving in the hardscrabble town in the southern province of Caqueta shortly after 8:30 a.m. (1330 GMT). Russian-made Mi-17 helicopters loaned to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) by Colombia's army had taken them from an undisclosed jungle location.

The soldiers were to give a news conference before noon, together with leaders of the so-called Southern Bloc of the Marxist-led Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC). The hostages' handover to members of the ICRC and Colombia's National Conciliation Commission was to follow.

Robert Pastor of the Carter Foundation in the United States -- one of several international observers on hand, including former Costa Rican President Rodrigo Carazo -- said he viewed the negotiated release as "important because it could be the chance to end Latin America's longest-running guerrilla war."

But Enrique Santos Calderon, news editor of Bogota's El Tiempo newspaper, predicted that the handover would only add to Colombia's internal conflict, since it underscored the growing strength of the guerrillas.
"This is a tactical, public relations and even diplomatic triumph for the FARC that will only increase their armed belligerence," he said.
The FARC, Latin America's largest and oldest guerrilla army, was founded as a Marxist, pro-Soviet group in 1964, but its roots go back to peasant militias formed in 1948.
"I'm in good health. Everything is fine. They treated us well," one of the first soldiers to arrive said to the cheers of onlookers in Cartagena del Chaira's main square.

"I'm glad to be here. It was tough being so long in the mountains," said another soldier, who wore a black-and-white baseball cap and gave his name as John Jairo. On entering the square, he raised his arms in triumph, drawing applause from the crowd, and made the sign of the cross on his chest.

The FARC's Aug. 30, 1996, raid on a jungle army base in neighbouring Putumayo Province, in which at least 27 soldiers were killed and 60 were captured, marked one of the group's biggest military victories.

It also dealt a humiliating blow to the army, leading Western military attaches to conclude that it had lost the momentum in Colombia's protracted conflict. A similar opinion emerged from a survey published in Bogota's El Espectador newspaper on Saturday in which 64 percent of participants said they thought the army was losing the war.
Cartagena del Chaira is a symbolic choice for the handover, since it is in the heart of an area noted since the early 1980s for the growing of coca, whose leaves are the raw material for cocaine.
The FARC has long been accused of protecting rural drug farms and laboratories. More recently the government has accused it of taking a direct role in drug production and trafficking.

After their news conference, the soldiers were due to be flown to a sprawling military base at Larandia, just outside the 5,000-square-mile (13,000-sq.-km) portion of Caqueta that President Ernesto Samper had ordered the army to demilitarize for the troops' release.
